https://www.dw.com/en/eu-seeks-ways-to-m.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nr5V Expansion was a key issue at 'Berlin Process' talks in candidate country Montenegro this month seeking to further Western Balkan integration into the EU Image: Regierung von Montenegro Advertisement The European Commission on Tuesday published a document called "Preparing for a wider Union," which sought to lay out new proposals on "the policy orientations and actions needed to prepare the [European] Union for future enlargements ." Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europe's future depends on the choices we make today," as she tries to encourage progress at the EU's leaders' summit this month and in other upcoming talks on the matter. The EU's executive proposed an array of changes — including a gradual integration process for would-be members, new safeguards "to ensure that commitments undertaken during accession negotiations continue to be fulfiled steadily after accession," and changes to voting rules. They were trying to strike a balance between simplifying the accession process, incentivizing candidate countries to continue to pursue it, and allaying concerns among existing members about potential risks or costs of expansion. Ukraine is the newest EU candidate country, seeking to accelerate the process amid Russia's invasion Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS Why is expansion coming back into focus? In the quarter century after the end of the Cold War, the EU rapidly grew from a union of 12 member states to 28, before dipping back down to 27 when the UK left following 2016's Brexit referendum. But the process has ground to a halt ever since, with a series of candidate countries stuck in lengthy negotiations and little apparent appetite among members to continue to expand. In recent years, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine and signs of the US vying for increased influence in parts of Europe, theoretical interest in expansion has picked up once more . But realizing the idea, with strict rules governing the accession process and the need for unanimous support among existing members for many core steps, has remained challenging. EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did the Commission say about expansion? Von der Leyen said the Commission was trying to prepare institutions, adapt policies and adjust budgets to reflect shared realities to better facilitate and accommodate expansion. "Enlargement of our Union is a geopolitical imperative," she said. "Today, we are laying the groundwork to ensure that a larger Union is also a stronger one: more resilient, more effective, and firmly anchored in the values and rules that define us." She said that as countries progress on their path towards reform, "the EU must be ready to welcome them." Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that Brussels' assessment "shows that the EU can accommodate a larger membership." But "there are areas where we see challenges we need to address," she acknowledged. "One is the rule of law and sincere cooperation, where we are proposing stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding, including reducing funding or restricting voting rights," Kos said. Why the US-EU rift is spilling into the Balkans To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What changes are the European Commission proposing? The Commission lays out a number of proposed changes or policies designed to smooth the accession process, including but not limited to: Moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting among members in a number of the less significant votes about advancing or progressing membership bids It makes no mention of changing the current requirement for a unanimous vote about finalizing membership applications, however Gradual and accelerated integration of candidate countries to "bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses," but which would remain "conditional and reversible" "Stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitements undertaken during the acession negotiations" in future accession treaties, which could "in the most serious cases" extend to the suspension of voting rights Introducing "targeted arrangements" to "significantly limit financial support and market access" for sensitive agricultural products from candidate country Ukraine Ukraine's vast agricultural sector had prompted some concerns among EU members looking at how the bloc's budget could handle expansion, given that agriculture is a rare policy area where the bulk of spending and subsidies are orchestrated at the EU level, not by national governments All these proposals will be subject to further discussion among European leaders and governments, with the next major meeting being next week's EU leaders' summit. Should they gain traction and progress, no doubt after some alterations and amendments along the way, they would ultimately have to face and pass various voting procedures to be implemented. Moldova's President Maia Sandu is also a staunch advocate of her country joining the EU Image: Vladislav Culiomza/REUTERS What's the current situation with EU candidate countries? A total of eight countries currently have formal candidate status, meaning they are seeking to join the EU and have at least begun the often lengthy process that involves. Some hope to join the bloc sooner rather than later, not least frontrunner Montenegro , after years of negotiations. Kos told DW last week that Montenegro was currently on track to become the next EU member by 2028. Others, like Turkey, have nominally been candidates for decades but have made no discernible progress for years. Ukraine is the newest addition to the list , having only gained full candidate status in 2024, but it is also the one with the most pressing motivation to hurry the process along amid Russia's invasion. Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, North Macedonia and Serbia are also all seeking membership. A ninth country, Kosovo, is recognized as a potential candidate but not a formal one — with not all EU members recognizing Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia . https://www.dw.com/en/australian-mp-seri.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OP08 Helen Haines was elected to the Australian parliament in 2019 Image: Mick Tsikas/AAP Image/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Australian police are investigating a suspected car attack that has left independent MP Helen Haines with critical injuries. Counterterrorism investigators have joined the probe following the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne. What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines? Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, said by police to be a white Toyota, outside her office, leaving her with serious injuries, particularly to her lower body. Broadcaster ABC cited witnesses as saying they had heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars. The driver, described as a 43-year-old man, has been arrested, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Investigators are reported to have found a knife in the car. Prime Minister Albanese has said the incident seemed 'no accident' Image: Marek Ladzinski/ZUMA/picture alliance Apparently deliberate attack: PM Albanese "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," Albanese told ABC. He said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence. "The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media." Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents." At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery." Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years. Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action. Spain: First footage reveals wreckage of deadly high-speed train crash Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 28 October 2026 - 12:16 GMT+1 At least 10 people died when a high-speed train struck another near Toledo, Spain. Two carriages derailed, leaving rescuers searching through the wreckage as authorities warned the death toll could rise. … More The crash occurred between Urda and Los Yébenes, in Toledo province , when a train travelling from Madrid towards Seville struck the rear of another that had stopped on the same track . Two carriages were knocked off the rails , one of them torn apart, with twisted metal and debris scattered down a gravel embankment. Aerial footage shows the damaged trains surrounded by firefighters, police and rescue teams in a flat, rural landscape. Castilla-La Mancha government spokeswoman Esther Padilla confirmed 10 deaths but warned that the toll was likely to rise . ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The collision involved a RENFE train carrying 397 passengers and an IRYO service with 147 people on board. The cause remains unknown . Emergency workers concentrated on reaching victims in the two worst-damaged carriages, while injured passengers were taken to nearby hospitals. A military emergency unit was deployed , and rail services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended . Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his engagements to focus on the disaster . It was Spain's second major rail tragedy of 2026 , following a January collision in southern Spain that killed 45 people . That earlier accident had already raised concerns about safety on the country's extensive high-speed rail network.
